claim: The membrane attack complex (MAC or C5b-9) is an important effector of the immune system to kill invading microbes.
source: The membrane attack complex (MAC or C5b-9) is an important effector of the immune system to kill invading microbes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the role of MAC in immunity.

claim: MAC formation is initiated when complement enzymes on the bacterial surface convert complement component C5 into C5b.
source: MAC formation is initiated when complement enzymes on the bacterial surface convert complement component C5 into C5b.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of MAC formation initiation.

claim: Soluble forms of MAC (sMAC), or terminal complement complex (TCC), are often detected in sera of patients suffering from infections.
source: Although the MAC is a membrane-inserted complex, soluble forms of MAC (sMAC), or terminal complement complex (TCC), are often detected in sera of patients suffering from infections.
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies in the introduction.

claim: sMAC has been proposed as a biomarker.
source: Consequently, sMAC has been proposed as a biomarker, but it remains unclear when and how it is formed during infections.
evidence: This is supported by references to clinical literature.

claim: It remains unclear when and how sMAC is formed during infections.
source: Consequently, sMAC has been proposed as a biomarker, but it remains unclear when and how it is formed during infections.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: sMAC is primarily formed in human serum by bacteria resistant to MAC-dependent killing.
source: Here, we studied mechanisms of MAC formation on different Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria and found that sMAC is primarily formed in human serum by bacteria resistant to MAC-dependent killing.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: C5 was converted into C5b more potently by MAC-resistant compared to MAC-sensitive Escherichia coli strains.
source: Surprisingly, C5 was converted into C5b more potently by MAC-resistant compared to MAC-sensitive Escherichia coli strains.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: MAC precursors are released from the surface of MAC-resistant bacteria during MAC assembly.
source: In addition, we found that MAC precursors are released from the surface of MAC-resistant bacteria during MAC assembly.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Release of MAC precursors from bacteria induced lysis of bystander human erythrocytes.
source: Although release of MAC precursors from bacteria induced lysis of bystander human erythrocytes, serum regulators vitronectin (Vn) and clusterin (Clu) can prevent this.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: Serum regulators vitronectin (Vn) and clusterin (Clu) can prevent bystander lysis of human erythrocytes induced by MAC precursors released from bacteria.
source: Although release of MAC precursors from bacteria induced lysis of bystander human erythrocytes, serum regulators vitronectin (Vn) and clusterin (Clu) can prevent this.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: sMAC released from bacteria in serum is a heterogeneous mixture of complexes composed of C5b-8, up to three copies of C9 and multiple copies of Vn and Clu.
source: Combining size exclusion chromatography with mass spectrometry profiling, we show that sMAC released from bacteria in serum is a heterogeneous mixture of complexes composed of C5b-8, up to three copies of C9 and multiple copies of Vn and Clu.
evidence: This is supported by SEC and MS data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The complement system consists of soluble plasma proteins that circulate as inactive precursors.
source: The complement system consists of soluble plasma proteins that circulate as inactive precursors (Gasque, 2004; Ricklin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: When complement is activated at the bacterial surface, a proteolytic cascade is triggered that labels the surface with convertase enzymes.
source: When complement is activated at the bacterial surface, a proteolytic cascade is triggered that labels the surface with convertase enzymes (Gasque, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Convertases initially convert C3 into anaphylatoxin C3a and C3b, labelling bacteria for phagocytosis by neutrophils.
source: These convertases initially convert C3 into anaphylatoxin C3a and C3b, labelling bacteria for phagocytosis by neutrophils (Merle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Convertases convert C5 into pro-inflammatory C5a, which recruits and activates neutrophils, and C5b.
source: As terminal step in the pathway, these convertases also convert C5 into pro-inflammatory C5a, which recruits and activates neutrophils, and C5b.
evidence: This is established knowledge about complement cascade.

claim: C5b, together with C6, C7, C8, and up to 18 copies of C9, assembles a large, ring-shaped membrane attack complex (MAC) pore.
source: C5b, together with C6, C7, C8, and up to 18 copies of C9, assembles a large, ring-shaped membrane attack complex (MAC) pore (Bhakdi and Tranum-Jensen, 1978; Müller-Eberhard, 1986; Menny et al., 2018; Doorduijn et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: MAC pores can efficiently kill Gram-negative bacteria.
source: MAC pores can efficiently kill Gram-negative bacteria, although some serum-resistant Gram-negative bacteria can survive killing by MAC pores (Joiner, 1988; Merino et al., 1992; Doorduijn et al., 2016; Abreu and Barbosa, 2017), and Gram-positive bacteria are intrinsically resistant to MAC-dependent killing (Brown, 1985).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Some serum-resistant Gram-negative bacteria can survive killing by MAC pores.
source: MAC pores can efficiently kill Gram-negative bacteria, although some serum-resistant Gram-negative bacteria can survive killing by MAC pores (Joiner, 1988; Merino et al., 1992; Doorduijn et al., 2016; Abreu and Barbosa, 2017), and Gram-positive bacteria are intrinsically resistant to MAC-dependent killing (Brown, 1985).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Gram-positive bacteria are intrinsically resistant to MAC-dependent killing.
source: MAC pores can efficiently kill Gram-negative bacteria, although some serum-resistant Gram-negative bacteria can survive killing by MAC pores (Joiner, 1988; Merino et al., 1992; Doorduijn et al., 2016; Abreu and Barbosa, 2017), and Gram-positive bacteria are intrinsically resistant to MAC-dependent killing (Brown, 1985).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Patients treated with C5 inhibitor eculizumab experience recurrent infections with Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Nevertheless, the clinical importance of the MAC in humans is made clear by recurrent infections with Gram-negative bacteria in patients treated with C5 inhibitor eculizumab (Heesterbeek et al., 2018) or patients with genetic deficiencies in one of the MAC components (Lewis and Ram, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical literature.

claim: Patients with genetic deficiencies in one of the MAC components experience recurrent infections with Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Nevertheless, the clinical importance of the MAC in humans is made clear by recurrent infections with Gram-negative bacteria in patients treated with C5 inhibitor eculizumab (Heesterbeek et al., 2018) or patients with genetic deficiencies in one of the MAC components (Lewis and Ram, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical literature.

claim: Complement activation products that are released into plasma during complement activation are frequently used as biomarkers for infections.
source: Complement activation products that are released into plasma during complement activation are frequently used as biomarkers for infections (Barnum et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: TCC or sMAC is often increased in plasma of patients suffering from bacterial infections.
source: One of these biomarkers is the terminal complement complex (TCC) or soluble MAC (sMAC), which is often increased in plasma of patients suffering from bacterial infections (Lin et al., 1993; Mook-Kanamori et al., 2014; Westra et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: It is unclear how sMAC is formed when complement is activated on bacteria.
source: However, since MAC is meant to assemble and insert in bacterial membranes, it is still unclear how sMAC is formed when complement is activated on bacteria (Mook-Kanamori et al., 2014).
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: sMAC could represent debris of lysed cells.
source: sMAC could represent debris of lysed cells, but could also represent improperly inserted MAC pores that are released from bacteria during complement activation (Morgan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis mentioned in the literature.

claim: sMAC could represent improperly inserted MAC pores that are released from bacteria during complement activation.
source: sMAC could represent debris of lysed cells, but could also represent improperly inserted MAC pores that are released from bacteria during complement activation (Morgan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis mentioned in the literature.

claim: Four E. coli strains (MG1655, BW25113, MC1061, and 547563.1) were killed in serum.
source: Bacterial viability was assessed by counting colony forming units (CFUs) and revealed that four strains were killed in serum (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Killing of MAC-sensitive E. coli strains was MAC-dependent because it could be inhibited with C5 inhibitors OmCI and eculizumab.
source: Killing was MAC-dependent because it could be inhibited with C5 inhibitors OmCI and eculizumab (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a), indicating that these strains are 'MAC-sensitive'.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Eight E. coli strains survived in serum.
source: The other eight strains survived in serum (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Three serum-resistant E. coli strains (552059.1, 552060.1, and 567705.1) showed C3b deposition similar to MAC-sensitive strains.
source: Deposition of C3b on the bacterial surface (Figure 1b) and release of C3a in the supernatant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b) were similar on three strains compared to the MAC-sensitive strains, indicating that these strains activate complement efficiently.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1b and ELISA data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Three serum-resistant E. coli strains (552059.1, 552060.1, and 567705.1) showed C3a release similar to MAC-sensitive strains.
source: Deposition of C3b on the bacterial surface (Figure 1b) and release of C3a in the supernatant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b) were similar on three strains compared to the MAC-sensitive strains, indicating that these strains activate complement efficiently.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: MAC components bind to MAC-resistant E. coli strains after complement activation.
source: We have previously shown that MAC components bind to these strains after complement activation (Doorduijn et al., 2021), suggesting that they are 'MAC-resistant' strains.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Five E. coli strains showed little to no deposition of C3b and were considered 'complement-resistant'.
source: The other five strains showed little to no deposition of C3b and were considered 'complement-resistant'.
evidence: This is based on C3b deposition data in Figure 1b.

claim: All tested MAC-resistant E. coli strains efficiently formed sMAC in serum.
source: All tested MAC-resistant strains efficiently formed sMAC in serum, whereas MAC-sensitive strains and most complement-resistant strains only generated slightly more sMAC than present in serum alone (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 1c.

claim: MAC-sensitive E. coli strains and most complement-resistant strains only generated slightly more sMAC than present in serum alone.
source: All tested MAC-resistant strains efficiently formed sMAC in serum, whereas MAC-sensitive strains and most complement-resistant strains only generated slightly more sMAC than present in serum alone (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 1c.

claim: MAC-resistant E. coli strain 552059.1 generated at least fivefold more sMAC compared to MAC-sensitive MG1655 or complement-resistant 547654.1.
source: Titration of the supernatant of MAC-resistant 552059.1 suggested that there was at least fivefold more sMAC compared to MAC-sensitive MG1655 or complement-resistant 547654.1 (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA titration data in Figure 1d.

claim: sMAC formation by E. coli was complement-dependent, since C5 inhibitor OmCI and eculizumab prevented formation of sMAC.
source: sMAC was formed in a complement-dependent manner, since C5 inhibitor OmCI and eculizumab prevented formation of sMAC (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Two MAC-resistant Klebsiella strains formed more sMAC in serum compared to MAC-sensitive Klebsiella strains.
source: Finally, two MAC-resistant Klebsiella strains also formed more sMAC in serum compared to MAC-sensitive Klebsiella strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c), suggesting that these findings can also be translated to other Gram-negative species.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c.

claim: The findings on sMAC formation by MAC-resistant bacteria can be translated to other Gram-negative species.
source: Finally, two MAC-resistant Klebsiella strains also formed more sMAC in serum compared to MAC-sensitive Klebsiella strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c), suggesting that these findings can also be translated to other Gram-negative species.
evidence: This is an inference based on Klebsiella data.

claim: sMAC is detected in plasma of patients that suffer from bacterial infections with Gram-positive bacteria.
source: However, sMAC is also detected in plasma of patients that suffer from bacterial infections with Gram-positive bacteria (Barnum et al., 2020; Lin et al., 1993; Mook-Kanamori et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: The thick peptidoglycan layer of Gram-positive bacteria is thought to be responsible for preventing MAC formation in the cytosolic membrane and bacterial killing.
source: This thick peptidoglycan layer is thought to be responsible for preventing MAC formation in the cytosolic membrane and bacterial killing (Brown, 1985).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: Three Staphylococcus aureus strains (SH1000, Wood46 and Newman), one Staphylococcus epidermidis strain (KV103), and one Streptococcus agalactiae strain (COH-1) activate complement and resist killing by MAC pores.
source: We have previously shown that these strains activate complement and resist killing by MAC pores (Berends et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: All five tested Gram-positive strains formed sMAC in serum.
source: sMAC was formed in all five Gram-positive strains (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 2.

claim: sMAC generation by Gram-positive strains was three- to fivefold higher compared to MAC-sensitive E. coli MG1655.
source: sMAC generation was three- to fivefold higher for Gram-positive strains compared to MAC-sensitive E. coli MG1655 (Figure 2), corresponding more or less with the difference observed for MAC-resistant E. coli (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 2.

claim: MAC-resistant E. coli strains converted all C5 in serum.
source: Western blotting of the serum supernatant confirmed that MAC-resistant strains converted all C5 in serum (Figure 3a), whereas leftover C5 was still visible for MAC-sensitive strains.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 3a.

claim: Leftover C5 was still visible for MAC-sensitive E. coli strains after serum incubation.
source: Western blotting of the serum supernatant confirmed that MAC-resistant strains converted all C5 in serum (Figure 3a), whereas leftover C5 was still visible for MAC-sensitive strains.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 3a.

claim: MAC-resistant E. coli strains generated approximately fivefold more C5a compared to MAC-sensitive strains.
source: A sandwich ELISA was also used to quantify the released C5a into serum supernatant, which revealed that MAC-resistant strains generated ± fivefold more C5a compared to MAC-sensitive strains (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 3b.

claim: The difference in C5a generation between MAC-resistant and MAC-sensitive E. coli was comparable to the difference in sMAC.
source: A sandwich ELISA was also used to quantify the released C5a into serum supernatant, which revealed that MAC-resistant strains generated ± fivefold more C5a compared to MAC-sensitive strains (Figure 3b). This was comparable to the difference in sMAC (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing data from Figures 3b and 1d.

claim: Gram-positive bacteria that generated sMAC also generated more C5a compared to MAC-sensitive E. coli MG1655.
source: Gram-positive bacteria that generated sMAC (Figure 2) also generated more C5a compared to MAC-sensitive MG1655 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), although this difference in C5a generation was smaller (±threefold) compared to the difference between MAC-resistant and MAC-sensitive E. coli (±tenfold, Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The difference in C5a generation by Gram-positive bacteria compared to MAC-sensitive E. coli was smaller (approximately threefold) than the difference between MAC-resistant and MAC-sensitive E. coli (approximately tenfold).
source: Gram-positive bacteria that generated sMAC (Figure 2) also generated more C5a compared to MAC-sensitive MG1655 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), although this difference in C5a generation was smaller (±threefold) compared to the difference between MAC-resistant and MAC-sensitive E. coli (±tenfold, Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by comparing ELISA data from Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3b.

claim: The three tested MAC-resistant E. coli strains express LPS O-antigen.
source: We have previously shown that the three tested MAC-resistant strains express O-Ag (Doorduijn et al., 2021), whereas only one out of four MAC-sensitive strains (547563.1) does as well (shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, summarized in Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and silver staining data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Only one out of four MAC-sensitive E. coli strains (547563.1) expresses LPS O-antigen.
source: We have previously shown that the three tested MAC-resistant strains express O-Ag (Doorduijn et al., 2021), whereas only one out of four MAC-sensitive strains (547563.1) does as well (shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, summarized in Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by silver staining data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: MAC-sensitive Klebsiella strains show little detectable O-Ag compared to MAC-resistant Klebsiella strains.
source: Silver staining of O-Ag for Klebsiella strains suggested a comparable trend, showing little detectable O-Ag for MAC-sensitive strains compared to MAC-resistant strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by silver staining data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Expression of O-Ag increased C5a generation in the supernatant 10-fold.
source: Expression of O-Ag increased C5a generation in the supernatant 10-fold (Figure 3c) and sMAC release 3.5-fold (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data comparing O-Ag negative and positive strains in Figure 3c.

claim: Expression of O-Ag increased sMAC release 3.5-fold.
source: Expression of O-Ag increased C5a generation in the supernatant 10-fold (Figure 3c) and sMAC release 3.5-fold (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data comparing O-Ag negative and positive strains in Figure 3d.

claim: C3b deposition on the bacterial surface was comparable both in the presence and absence of O-Ag in serum.
source: C3b deposition on the bacterial surface was comparable both in the presence and absence of O-Ag in serum (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c), suggesting that initial complement activation was not affected by the expression of O-Ag, similar to other MAC-resistant E. coli (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Initial complement activation was not affected by the expression of O-Ag.
source: C3b deposition on the bacterial surface was comparable both in the presence and absence of O-Ag in serum (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c), suggesting that initial complement activation was not affected by the expression of O-Ag, similar to other MAC-resistant E. coli (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is an inference based on C3b deposition data.

claim: Expression of O-Ag on E. coli can increase C5a generation and sMAC release in serum.
source: Therefore, these data indicate that expression of O-Ag on E. coli can increase C5a generation and sMAC release in serum.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: MAC pores assemble in a stepwise manner.
source: MAC pores assemble in a stepwise manner.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MAC assembly.

claim: C5b binds to C6 to form a stable C5b6 complex.
source: C5b binds to C6 to form a stable C5b6 complex, which next binds C7 to anchor the C5b-7 complex to the membrane of bacteria (Preissner et al., 1985).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: C5b6 binds C7 to anchor the C5b-7 complex to the membrane of bacteria.
source: C5b binds to C6 to form a stable C5b6 complex, which next binds C7 to anchor the C5b-7 complex to the membrane of bacteria (Preissner et al., 1985).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Binding of C8 inserts the nascent MAC into the bacterial cell envelope.
source: Finally, binding of C8 inserts the nascent MAC into the bacterial cell envelope, and is more tightly inserted when C9 binds and polymerizes a transmembrane ring (Bayly-Jones et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The nascent MAC is more tightly inserted when C9 binds and polymerizes a transmembrane ring.
source: Finally, binding of C8 inserts the nascent MAC into the bacterial cell envelope, and is more tightly inserted when C9 binds and polymerizes a transmembrane ring (Bayly-Jones et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: More C5 was converted into C5b for MAC-resistant E. coli 552059.1 compared to MAC-sensitive MG1655.
source: Western blotting of the supernatant revealed that more C5 was converted into C5b for MAC-resistant 552059.1 compared to MAC-sensitive MG1655 (Figure 4b, indicated by the orange and blue arrow), in line with Figure 4b.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4b.

claim: Binding of C7 to the nascent MAC prevented release of C5b6 from the bacterial surface.
source: Western blotting revealed that binding of C7 to the nascent MAC prevented release of C5b6 from the bacterial surface (Figure 4b), as was previously observed for MAC-sensitive MG1655 (Doorduijn et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4b and citation to previous work.

claim: Binding of C7 appeared to increase C5 conversion on MAC-resistant E. coli 552059.1.
source: Binding of C7 also appeared to increase C5 conversion on MAC-resistant 552059.1 (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is an observation from Western blot data in Figure 4b.

claim: Binding of C8 to the nascent MAC triggered release of C5b from MAC-resistant E. coli 552059.1, even in the presence of final MAC component C9.
source: However, binding of C8 to the nascent MAC triggered release of C5b from MAC-resistant 552059.1, even in the presence of final MAC component C9 (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4b.

claim: Binding of C8 triggered some release of C5b from the surface of MAC-sensitive MG1655, but this was prevented when C9 was also present.
source: Binding of C8 triggered some release of C5b from the surface of MAC-sensitive MG1655, but this was prevented when C9 was also present (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4b.

claim: Binding of C8 and C9 released fourfold more C5b6 from the surface of MAC-resistant E. coli compared to MAC-sensitive E. coli.
source: Quantification of C5b6 by ELISA revealed that binding of C8 and C9 released fourfold more C5b6 from the surface of MAC-resistant E. coli (Figure 4c and d).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figures 4c and 4d.

claim: Binding of C8 and C9 to C5b-7 triggers release of the nascent MAC from MAC-resistant E. coli.
source: These data suggest that binding of C8 and C9 to C5b-7 triggers release of the nascent MAC from MAC-resistant E. coli.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Complement activation on erythrocytes can cause MAC-dependent lysis of bystander cells that are not recognized by the complement system.
source: Previous reports showed that complement activation on erythrocytes can cause MAC-dependent lysis of bystander cells that are not recognized by the complement system, the so-called bystander lysis (Lachmann and Thompson, 1970; Götze and Müller-Eberhard, 1970; Cooper and Müller-Eberhard, 1970).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Complement activation and subsequent release of MAC precursors from MAC-resistant E. coli resulted in lysis of bystander erythrocytes for all MAC-resistant E. coli strains and MAC-sensitive 547563.1.
source: This resulted in lysis of bystander erythrocytes for all MAC-resistant E. coli strains and MAC-sensitive 547563.1 (Figure 5b), corresponding with the production of sMAC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by bystander lysis assay data in Figure 5b.

claim: Bystander lysis of erythrocytes was prevented in the presence of C5 conversion inhibitor OmCI.
source: Lysis was prevented in the presence of C5 conversion inhibitor OmCI (Figure 5b), suggesting that lysis was MAC-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5b.

claim: Bystander lysis of erythrocytes by MAC precursors released from E. coli was MAC-dependent.
source: Lysis was prevented in the presence of C5 conversion inhibitor OmCI (Figure 5b), suggesting that lysis was MAC-dependent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effect of C5 inhibitor.

claim: Release of MAC precursors from E. coli can result in lysis of bystander human cells.
source: These data show that release of MAC precursors from E. coli can result in lysis of bystander human cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: MAC-resistant E. coli 552059.1 did not trigger bystander lysis of erythrocytes in a human serum environment.
source: However, when we studied bystander lysis in a human serum environment, we observed that the 552059.1 did not trigger bystander lysis of erythrocytes (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5c.

claim: Vn and Clu are known to scavenge and inactivate sMAC.
source: Serum regulators Vn and Clu are known to scavenge and inactivate sMAC (Zipfel and Skerka, 2009; Schmidt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Both Vn and Clu inhibited bystander lysis of erythrocytes when MAC assembled on convertase-labelled E. coli 552059.1 at concentrations representative for 10% serum.
source: Indeed, both Vn and Clu inhibited bystander lysis of erythrocytes when MAC assembled on convertase-labelled E. coli 552059.1 (as described in Figure 5a) at concentrations representative for 10% serum (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5c.

claim: Clu, but not Vn, prevents the formation of polymeric-C9 in the supernatant.
source: SDS-PAGE revealed that Clu, but not Vn, prevents the formation of polymeric-C9 in the supernatant (Figure 5—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Vn and Clu interfere at different stages in the assembly of sMAC.
source: This suggests that Vn and Clu interfere at different stages in the assembly of sMAC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects on C9 polymerization.

claim: Vn and Clu did not inhibit binding of C9 when MAC was assembled by local conversion of C5 on convertase-labelled MAC-sensitive MG1655.
source: Vn and Clu both specifically prevent lysis of bystander cells by MAC, since Vn and Clu did not inhibit binding of C9 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b), or MAC-dependent killing (Figure 5—figure supplement 2c) when MAC was assembled by local conversion of C5 on convertase-labelled MAC-sensitive MG1655.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Vn and Clu did not inhibit MAC-dependent killing when MAC was assembled by local conversion of C5 on convertase-labelled MAC-sensitive MG1655.
source: Vn and Clu both specifically prevent lysis of bystander cells by MAC, since Vn and Clu did not inhibit binding of C9 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b), or MAC-dependent killing (Figure 5—figure supplement 2c) when MAC was assembled by local conversion of C5 on convertase-labelled MAC-sensitive MG1655.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Vn and Clu specifically prevent lysis of bystander cells by MAC.
source: Vn and Clu both specifically prevent lysis of bystander cells by MAC, since Vn and Clu did not inhibit binding of C9 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b), or MAC-dependent killing (Figure 5—figure supplement 2c) when MAC was assembled by local conversion of C5 on convertase-labelled MAC-sensitive MG1655.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Release of MAC precursors from E. coli can trigger lysis of bystander human erythrocytes, but serum regulators Vn and Clu can inhibit this bystander lysis.
source: Altogether, our data suggest that release of MAC precursors from E. coli can trigger lysis of bystander human erythrocytes, but that serum regulators Vn and Clu can inhibit this bystander lysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: Commercially available sMAC used in the study consists of C5b-8, one to three copies of C9 and several copies of Vn and Clu.
source: Menny et al., 2021 recently reported that the commercially available sMAC used in our study consists of C5b-8, one to three copies of C9 and several copies of Vn and Clu, using proteomics, cross-linking MS, and cryo-electron microscopy.
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: Most bacterial sMAC eluted later from the SEC column than commercial sMAC.
source: The total amount of sMAC components that were detected with LC-MS/MS in individual fractions (Figure 6c and Figure 6—figure supplement 1b,c) corresponded with BN-PAGE (Figure 6b), suggesting that most bacterial sMAC eluted later from the SEC column than commercial sMAC.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing LC-MS/MS and BN-PAGE data.

claim: For both bacterial and commercial sMAC, sMAC components C5, C7, and C8 were present in equal amounts in a pooled sample of fractions B5-B12.
source: For both bacterial and commercial sMAC, sMAC components C5, C7, and C8 were present in equal amounts in a pooled sample of fractions B5-B12 (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 6d.

claim: C6 and Vn were both twofold more abundant in bacterial sMAC compared to commercial sMAC.
source: However, C6 and Vn were both twofold more abundant for bacterial sMAC (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 6d.

claim: The increased ratio of C6 in bacterial sMAC is likely explained by the fact that not all monomeric-C6 could be separated during SEC.
source: The increased ratio of C6 is likely explained by the fact that not all monomeric-C6 could be separated during SEC (as was visible in fraction B9-B12 by BN-PAGE in Figure 6b).
evidence: This is an inference based on BN-PAGE data.

claim: Bacterial sMAC contained on average less C9 per C5 (ratio of 2:1) than commercially available sMAC (ratio of 3:1).
source: Surprisingly, bacterial sMAC contained on average less C9 per C5 (Figure 6d, ratio of 2:1) than commercially available sMAC (Figure 6d, ratio of 3:1).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 6d.

claim: The relative amount of C9 per C5 decreased in fractions that eluted later from the SEC column for bacterial sMAC.
source: The relative amount of C9 per C5 (Figure 6e), but not other sMAC components (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d), decreased in fractions that eluted later from the SEC column for bacterial sMAC.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 6e.

claim: The relative amount of C9 per C5 did not decrease in later fractions for commercially available sMAC.
source: This was not observed for commercially available sMAC (Figure 6f and Figure 6—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 6f.

claim: sMAC generated by bacteria contains more complexes with less C9 compared to commercial sMAC.
source: These data suggest that sMAC generated by bacteria contains more complexes with less C9 compared to commercial sMAC.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on LC-MS/MS data in Figure 6.

claim: Upon activation with S. aureus Wood46, the profiles of all sMAC components largely co-elute and are shifted to fractions that correspond to the higher mass range.
source: Upon activation, the profiles of all sMAC components largely co-elute and are shifted to fractions that correspond to the higher mass range.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS profiling data in Figure 7.

claim: Close to no monomeric MAC components were detected after incubation of serum with S. aureus Wood46.
source: In fact, close to no monomeric MAC components were detected after incubation with bacteria, suggesting that all available MAC components were incorporated into hetero-oligomeric sMAC complexes.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS profiling data in Figure 7.

claim: All available MAC components were incorporated into hetero-oligomeric sMAC complexes after incubation of serum with S. aureus Wood46.
source: In fact, close to no monomeric MAC components were detected after incubation with bacteria, suggesting that all available MAC components were incorporated into hetero-oligomeric sMAC complexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of monomeric components.

claim: No sMAC without Vn and Clu was observed in the bacterial activated sample.
source: We did not observe any sMAC without Vn and Clu in the bacterial activated sample, since these would be located around the 664 kDa molecular weight marker, suggesting that all sMAC complexes were bound to multiple Vn and Clu molecules (corresponding with the relative abundance in Figure 6d).
evidence: This is an observation from SEC-MS data in Figure 7.

claim: All sMAC complexes generated by S. aureus Wood46 were bound to multiple Vn and Clu molecules.
source: We did not observe any sMAC without Vn and Clu in the bacterial activated sample, since these would be located around the 664 kDa molecular weight marker, suggesting that all sMAC complexes were bound to multiple Vn and Clu molecules (corresponding with the relative abundance in Figure 6d).
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of sMAC at the expected molecular weight for complexes without regulators.

claim: sMAC complexes generated by S. aureus Wood46 correlate with a ratio of one to three C9 molecules and an average of two C9 molecules to C5b-8.
source: The complexes correlate with a ratio of one to three C9 molecules and an average of two C9 molecules to C5b-8, with Clu as the most abundant regulator bound to sMAC.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS profiling data in Figure 7.

claim: Clu is the most abundant regulator bound to sMAC generated by S. aureus Wood46.
source: The complexes correlate with a ratio of one to three C9 molecules and an average of two C9 molecules to C5b-8, with Clu as the most abundant regulator bound to sMAC.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS profiling data in Figure 7.

claim: sMAC released from bacteria is a heterogeneous assembly comprising a single copy of C5b-8 together with multiple copies of C9, Clu and Vn in a mixture of stoichiometries.
source: Altogether, these data confirm that sMAC released from bacteria is a heterogeneous assembly comprising a single copy of C5b-8 together with multiple copies of C9, Clu and Vn in a mixture of stoichiometries.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on SEC and MS data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Detection of sMAC in human serum indicates potent C5 conversion by MAC-resistant bacteria.
source: These findings suggest that detection of sMAC in human serum indicates potent C5 conversion by MAC-resistant bacteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Increased C5 conversion has previously been associated with MAC resistance on Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Increased C5 conversion has previously been associated with MAC resistance on Gram-negative bacteria (Joiner et al., 1982a; Krukonis and Thomson, 2020), but this has not yet been directly linked to the detection of sMAC in human serum.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Increased C5 conversion has not yet been directly linked to the detection of sMAC in human serum.
source: Increased C5 conversion has previously been associated with MAC resistance on Gram-negative bacteria (Joiner et al., 1982a; Krukonis and Thomson, 2020), but this has not yet been directly linked to the detection of sMAC in human serum.
evidence: This identifies a novel contribution of the study.

claim: Potent C5 conversion by MAC-resistant E. coli is linked to the expression of LPS O-Ag.
source: On Gram-negative bacteria, we observed that potent C5 conversion by MAC-resistant E. coli is linked to the expression LPS O-Ag (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Cell envelope constituents, and in the case of Gram-negative bacteria specifically LPS O-Ag, can affect total C5 conversion.
source: Nonetheless, this suggests that cell envelope constituents, and in the case of Gram-negative bacteria specifically LPS O-Ag, can affect total C5 conversion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings.

claim: Linking Salmonella LPS O-Ag to sheep erythrocyte membranes can increase C3 consumption.
source: Grossman et al. have previously demonstrated that linking Salmonella LPS O-Ag to sheep erythrocyte membranes can increase C3 consumption (Grossman et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The density of C3b is important for the conversion of C5.
source: For the conversion of C5, however, the density of C3b is known to be important (Rawal and Pangburn, 2001; Berends et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Local densities of C3b might differ between MAC-sensitive and MAC-resistant E. coli, which could affect C5 convertase activity.
source: Although C3b deposition was comparable for MAC-sensitive and MAC-resistant E. coli, we cannot exclude that local densities of C3b might differ, which could affect C5 convertase activity and explain a difference in C5 conversion.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: sMAC is initially formed on the bacterial surface, but released as the nascent MAC further assembles.
source: Our findings suggest that sMAC is initially formed on the bacterial surface, but released as the nascent MAC further assembles.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Most sMAC complexes ultimately contain on average one to three C9 molecules and a varying amount of Vn and Clu copies.
source: Our MS data show that most sMAC complexes ultimately contain on average one to three C9 molecules and a varying amount of Vn and Clu copies, which implies that sMAC further assembles in solution.
evidence: This is supported by MS data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: sMAC further assembles in solution after being released from bacteria.
source: Our MS data show that most sMAC complexes ultimately contain on average one to three C9 molecules and a varying amount of Vn and Clu copies, which implies that sMAC further assembles in solution.
evidence: This is an inference based on MS data.

claim: Binding of C8 to C5b-7 on a MAC-resistant Salmonella minnesota strain triggered release of C5b-8.
source: Joiner et al. have previously observed that binding of C8 to C5b-7 on a MAC-resistant Salmonella minnesota strain triggered release of C5b-8 (Joiner et al., 1982b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Binding of C8 to soluble C5b-7 prevents binding to membranes.
source: Although binding of C8 to soluble C5b-7 prevents binding to membranes (Nemerow et al., 1979), our data suggest that released MAC precursors can still bind to bystander cells and form lytic MAC pores.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Released MAC precursors can still bind to bystander cells and form lytic MAC pores.
source: Although binding of C8 to soluble C5b-7 prevents binding to membranes (Nemerow et al., 1979), our data suggest that released MAC precursors can still bind to bystander cells and form lytic MAC pores.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the bystander lysis data.

claim: C5b-8 can immediately bind bystander cells in the assays, which prevents C5b-7 from entering a soluble state.
source: It is possible that C5b-8 can immediately bind bystander cells in our assays, which prevents C5b-7 from entering a soluble state.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Trace amounts of intermediate MAC precursors, such as C5b6, are also released from the bacterial surface and can form enough MAC pores to lyse bystander erythrocytes.
source: However, we cannot exclude that trace amounts of intermediate MAC precursors, such as C5b6, that are also released from the bacterial surface and can still form enough MAC pores to lyse bystander erythrocytes.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism.

claim: The nascent MAC is released because it is less capable of inserting into the bacterial cell envelope of MAC-resistant bacteria.
source: Since C8 and C9 are the MAC components that insert into membranes (Menny et al., 2018; Sharp et al., 2016), our findings suggest that the nascent MAC is released because it is less capable of inserting into the bacterial cell envelope of MAC-resistant bacteria.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings and established knowledge.

claim: The dense peptidoglycan layer of Gram-positive bacteria prevents insertion of MAC into the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: On Gram-positive bacteria, it is believed that the dense peptidoglycan layer prevents insertion of MAC into the cytoplasmic membrane (Brown, 1985).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: MAC resistance and improper insertion of MAC into the bacterial outer membrane have previously been linked to the expression and length of the LPS O-Ag.
source: On Gram-negative bacteria, MAC resistance and improper insertion of MAC into the bacterial outer membrane have previously been linked to the expression and length of the LPS O-Ag (Grossman et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The expression of LPS O-Ag directly increases the generation and release of sMAC.
source: We here show that the expression of LPS O-Ag directly increases the generation and release of sMAC (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: LPS O-Ag could prevent MAC proteins from inserting into hydrophobic patches of the bacterial outer membrane, ultimately resulting in release of sMAC.
source: LPS O-Ag could prevent MAC proteins from inserting into hydrophobic patches of the bacterial outer membrane, ultimately resulting in release of sMAC.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Expression of O-Ag impairs polymerization of C9 at the bacterial surface.
source: This is in line with our previous study, which demonstrated that expression of O-Ag impairs polymerization of C9 at the bacterial surface (Doorduijn et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The presence of LPS O-Ag could prevent binding of complement-activating antibodies that bind to epitopes close to the bacterial surface.
source: The presence of LPS O-Ag could also prevent binding of complement-activating antibodies that bind to epitopes close to the bacterial surface (Russo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation.

claim: Antibodies that recognize the O-Ag could activate complement further away from the surface, which prevents insertion of MAC proteins into outer membrane and results in release of sMAC.
source: Instead, antibodies that recognize the O-Ag could activate complement further away from the surface, which prevents insertion of MAC proteins into outer membrane and results in release of sMAC.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism.

claim: Vn and Clu are important in preventing lysis of bystander host cells when bacteria activate complement.
source: Findings in this study also highlight the importance of Vn and Clu in preventing lysis of bystander host cells when bacteria activate complement.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: In the absence of Vn and Clu, release of MAC precursors from bacteria resulted in lysis of bystander human erythrocytes.
source: In the absence of Vn and Clu, release of MAC precursors from bacteria resulted in lysis of bystander human erythrocytes (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: Vn and Clu did not prevent MAC-dependent killing of the target bacterium.
source: Importantly, Vn and Clu did not prevent MAC-dependent killing of the target bacterium, suggesting that Vn and Clu specifically inhibit bystander lysis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Complement activation on Streptococcus pneumoniae caused bystander lysis of chicken erythrocytes.
source: In these reports, complement activation on Streptococcus pneumoniae (Geelen et al., 1992) and Moraxella catarrhalis (Verduin et al., 1994) caused bystander lysis of chicken erythrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Complement activation on Moraxella catarrhalis caused bystander lysis of chicken erythrocytes.
source: In these reports, complement activation on Streptococcus pneumoniae (Geelen et al., 1992) and Moraxella catarrhalis (Verduin et al., 1994) caused bystander lysis of chicken erythrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Human erythrocytes are sensitive to bystander lysis induced by bacterial complement activation.
source: We here extend on these findings showing that human erythrocytes are also sensitive to bystander lysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Under physiological conditions, Vn and Clu are present in a two- to eightfold molar excess compared to MAC components in serum.
source: Under physiological conditions, Vn and Clu are present in a two- to eightfold molar excess compared to MAC components in serum, favoring inactivation of released MAC over binding to a bystander cell membrane (Barnum et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The molar excess of Vn and Clu over MAC components favors inactivation of released MAC over binding to a bystander cell membrane.
source: Under physiological conditions, Vn and Clu are present in a two- to eightfold molar excess compared to MAC components in serum, favoring inactivation of released MAC over binding to a bystander cell membrane (Barnum et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on the relative concentrations.

claim: Bystander lysis is not observed in serum of healthy donors.
source: Correspondingly, we do not observe bystander lysis in a serum of healthy donors in our study.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5c.

claim: Clu is decreased in plasma of children suffering from bacterial infections.
source: However, Willems et al., 2019 have recently reported that Clu is decreased in plasma of children suffering from bacterial infections.
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: Vn and Clu polymorphisms have been identified that impair their potency in scavenging and inactivating sMAC precursors.
source: Vn and Clu polymorphisms have also been identified that impair their potency in scavenging and inactivating sMAC precursors (Ståhl et al., 2009; van den Heuvel et al., 2018), which could predispose to host cell damage by bystander lysis.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Vn and Clu polymorphisms could predispose to host cell damage by bystander lysis.
source: Vn and Clu polymorphisms have also been identified that impair their potency in scavenging and inactivating sMAC precursors (Ståhl et al., 2009; van den Heuvel et al., 2018), which could predispose to host cell damage by bystander lysis.
evidence: This is speculation based on the polymorphism data.

claim: Patients with Vn and Clu polymorphisms suffered from recurrent complement-mediated hemolytic uremic syndrome.
source: For both polymorphisms, patients suffered from recurrent complement-mediated hemolytic uremic syndrome, and in case of the Vn polymorphism, this was even associated with recurrent E. coli infections.
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: The Vn polymorphism was associated with recurrent E. coli infections.
source: For both polymorphisms, patients suffered from recurrent complement-mediated hemolytic uremic syndrome, and in case of the Vn polymorphism, this was even associated with recurrent E. coli infections.
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacterial pathogens are known to recruit Vn to their surface.
source: Moreover, both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacterial pathogens are known to recruit Vn to their surface (Singh et al., 2010; Riesbeck, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: For Gram-negative bacteria, recruitment of Vn is thought to prevent MAC-dependent killing.
source: For Gram-negative bacteria, this is thought to prevent MAC-dependent killing (Hallström et al., 2009; Griffiths et al., 2011), but for Gram-positive bacteria, the purpose of recruiting Vn and Clu has remained elusive.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: For Gram-positive bacteria, the purpose of recruiting Vn and Clu has remained elusive.
source: For Gram-negative bacteria, this is thought to prevent MAC-dependent killing (Hallström et al., 2009; Griffiths et al., 2011), but for Gram-positive bacteria, the purpose of recruiting Vn and Clu has remained elusive.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: The study suggests a potential role of bystander lysis during bacterial infections that merits further investigation.
source: Altogether, our study therefore suggests a potential role of bystander lysis during bacterial infections that merits further investigation.
evidence: This is a conclusion and suggestion for future research.

claim: sMAC generated by bacteria is a heterogeneous mixture of alike protein complexes with different stoichiometries.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that sMAC generated by bacteria is a heterogeneous mixture of alike protein complexes with different stoichiometries.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on SEC and MS data.

claim: sMAC is believed to consist of C5b-7, C8, multiple copies of C9, and several copies of Vn and Clu.
source: sMAC is believed to consist of C5b-7, C8, multiple copies of C9, and several copies of Vn and Clu (Barnum et al., 2020; Preissner et al., 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: sMAC generated by zymosan particles in serum contains at least one to three copies of C9.
source: This was recently supported by Menny et al., 2021, who revealed that sMAC generated by zymosan particles in serum contains at least one to three copies of C9.
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: sMAC generated by bacteria is present in similar stoichiometries to commercial sMAC, but on average contains less C9 molecules, especially for sMAC generated by MAC-resistant E. coli.
source: Our data suggest that sMAC generated by bacteria is present in similar stoichiometries, but on average, contains less C9 molecules, especially for sMAC generated by MAC-resistant E. coli (Figures 6 and 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on MS data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The stoichiometry of sMAC could depend on the target cell that activates complement.
source: This suggests that the stoichiometry of sMAC could depend on the target cell that activates complement.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed differences.

claim: Complexes with less C9 might be lost during purification of commercially available sMAC.
source: However, it is important to note the possibility that complexes with less C9 are lost during purification of commercially available sMAC.
evidence: This is speculation about a technical limitation.

claim: Multiple copies of Vn and Clu are present in sMAC generated by bacteria.
source: Our data also show the presence of multiple copies of Vn and Clu in sMAC generated by bacteria, with Clu being the most abundant chaperone.
evidence: This is supported by MS data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Vn and Clu can efficiently capture all sMAC that is released in serum.
source: These findings suggest that Vn and Clu can efficiently capture all sMAC that is released in serum.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of regulators in all sMAC complexes.

claim: Clu binds and traps the terminal C9 in an intermediate conformation, thereby preventing further C9 polymerization.
source: This is in line with the recent structure of sMAC by Menny et al., 2021, which revealed that Clu binds and traps the terminal C9 in an intermediate conformation, thereby preventing further C9 polymerization.
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent structural work.

claim: Clu, and not Vn, is able to inhibit C9 polymerization.
source: This is also in line with our results showing that Clu, and not Vn, is able to inhibit C9 polymerization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2a.

claim: More Vn was detected in sMAC generated by bacteria compared to commercial sMAC.
source: Finally, compared to commercial sMAC, more Vn was detected in sMAC generated by bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by MS data in Figure 6d.

claim: The difference in Vn content between bacterial and commercial sMAC could be caused by a difference in the target cell that activates complement.
source: It is unclear if this is caused by a difference in the target cell that activates complement, or a difference in the serum that was used to generate sMAC.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of the difference.

claim: The difference in Vn content between bacterial and commercial sMAC could be caused by a difference in the serum that was used to generate sMAC.
source: It is unclear if this is caused by a difference in the target cell that activates complement, or a difference in the serum that was used to generate sMAC.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of the difference.

claim: The concentration of Vn in serum can vary largely between individuals.
source: The concentration of Vn in serum can vary largely between individuals (Barnum et al., 2020) and could be responsible for the observed difference.
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: sMAC represents an inactivated complex that is primarily released from MAC-resistant bacteria that potently activate complement.
source: Altogether, we show that sMAC represents an inactivated complex that is primarily released from MAC-resistant bacteria that potently activate complement.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The findings are clinically relevant as they provide insight into what sMAC as a biomarker could represent during bacterial infections.
source: These findings are clinically relevant as they provide insight into what sMAC as a biomarker could represent during bacterial infections.
evidence: This is a statement about the clinical relevance of the findings.

claim: Future clinical studies could determine if sMAC detection in the plasma of patients that suffer from bacterial infections correlates with potent complement activation and MAC resistance of the causative bacterial pathogen.
source: Future clinical studies could determine if sMAC detection in the plasma of patients that suffer from bacterial infections also correlates with potent complement activation and MAC resistance of the causative bacterial pathogen.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: These insights could enhance our understanding of the role of complement activation in the pathogenesis of bacterial infections.
source: These insights could enhance our understanding of the role of complement activation in the pathogenesis of bacterial infections.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential impact of the findings.
